titre: Grammaticalization: From going to to gonna
accroche: “Gonna” is not a lazy contraction of “going to”: it is a distinct grammatical word, with its own pronunciation rules.
contenu_vulgarise:
Originally, *going to* means only one thing: physically moving somewhere for a purpose. “I am going to town to buy bread” describes a real trip, followed by an intention. Nothing in this sentence yet announces a grammatical tense.

## A Verb of Motion That Loses the Motion

Between the 15th and 17th centuries, English gradually reanalyzes this construction. “I am going to buy bread” stops requiring real movement: you can say it sitting down, without moving an inch. The meaning of the verb *go*, the very idea of going somewhere, fades in favor of a quite different function: announcing what is going to happen. This is what linguists call grammaticalization: an ordinary word, loaded with concrete meaning, empties itself of that meaning (known as “semantic bleaching”) to become a grammatical tool, here, a future marker, alongside *will*.

## Proof in the Pronunciation Itself

The clearest trace of this shift is found in speakers' mouths, not in dictionaries. “I'm going to eat” is commonly contracted to “I'm gonna eat,” but “I'm going to the store,” which describes real movement toward a place, is never contracted to “I'm gonna the store”: the sentence sounds wrong to any native speaker. The phonetic reduction applies only where *going to* has ceased to mean movement; it stays blocked wherever the verb keeps its original meaning. Without knowing it, every speaker who says “gonna” applies a fine grammatical distinction, future versus motion, that no school rule ever taught them.

## What This Shifts

The phenomenon shifts the idea we have of grammar itself. The markers of tense, mood, or aspect that structure a language do not fall from the sky: they emerge, through wear, from ordinary everyday words. French does exactly the same thing, twice. The near future, “je vais chanter” (“I'm going to sing”), follows a path identical to that of *going to*: the verb *aller* has lost all sense of movement there. And the simple future itself, “je chanterai,” comes from the Latin fusion of the verb *habere*, to have, with the infinitive, *cantare habeo*, literally “I have to sing,” which became over the centuries a single ending. Grammar is therefore not a fixed system that one learns alongside vocabulary: it is yesterday's vocabulary, settled into layers.

repere.texte: English uses going to with a future value as early as the 15th century; by the 17th century, the construction is already well established as a grammatical marker, independent of any real movement, a complete semantic bleaching in two to three centuries.
repere.source: Danchev & Kytö, “The construction be going to + infinitive in Early Modern English,” 1994

carte.punch: “Gonna” is not a lazy contraction: it is a full-fledged grammatical word.
carte.idee: “Going to” originally meant real movement. English turns it into a future marker, emptied of its sense of motion. The proof is in the pronunciation: you say “I'm gonna eat,” never “I'm gonna the store”; the contraction exists only where the verb has lost its original meaning.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: More examples of the same mechanism in very different languages.

quiz.question: Why can you say “I'm gonna eat” but never “I'm gonna the store”?
choix: Because “the store” is a proper noun, which always blocks this kind of contraction in English
Because “gonna” is a purely colloquial spelling, never accepted before a place complement
Because the phonetic contraction depends on the length of the word following “going to” in the sentence
Because in the second sentence, “going to” keeps its original meaning of movement toward a place, without having become a future marker
quiz.explication: The reduction to “gonna” applies only where going to has lost its sense of movement to become a grammatical future marker; that is the case before a verb (“I'm gonna eat”), not before a place complement describing a real trip (“going to the store”). It has nothing to do with the length of the following word, proper-noun status, or a purely spelling restriction: it is a distinction of meaning, effortlessly respected by all speakers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the “going to” construction originally mean in English?
choix: A supposition about an uncertain future event
A moral obligation to do something
A real physical movement carried out for a specific purpose
A habit repeated in the recent past
quiz_supplementaire.explication: “I am going to town to buy bread” describes a real trip followed by an intention; nothing in this original sentence yet announces a grammatical tense.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other example of grammaticalization does French present, according to the card, besides the near future?
choix: The simple future, from the Latin fusion of the verb habere with the infinitive
The passé composé, from the fusion of the verb être with the past participle
The conditional, from the fusion of the verb pouvoir with the subjunctive
The imperfect, from the fusion of the verb aller with the present infinitive
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The simple future, “je chanterai,” comes from the Latin fusion cantare habeo, “I have to sing,” which became over the centuries a single verb ending.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do linguists call the process by which “going to” loses its sense of movement?
choix: Lexicalization of a simple verb form
Grammaticalization, with semantic bleaching of the verb
Creolization of a construction borrowed from another language
Morphological reduplication of a common verb stem
quiz_supplementaire.explication: This process, grammaticalization, empties the verb of its concrete sense of movement to make it a simple future marker, alongside will.
